2002A16.goal: $a+1=b+2=c+3=d+4=a+b+c+d+5$. We want $S=a+b+c+d$. Call the common value $k$ and write everything in terms of $k$.
2002A16.recognize: Chains of equal expressions: name the common value.

2002A17.goal: Cup 1: $4$ oz coffee; cup 2: $4$ oz cream. Pour half of cup 1 into cup 2, mix, pour half of cup 2 back. We want the cream fraction in cup 1. Track amounts.

tools.name: Mixture tracking
tools.fact: \text{a well-mixed half carries half of each ingredient}

2002A17.approach: After step 1: cup 1 has $2$ coffee; cup 2 has $2$ coffee $+4$ cream. Pouring $3$ oz back brings $1$ coffee and $2$ cream. Cup 1: $3$ coffee, $2$ cream.

steps.title: First pour
steps.explain: Cup 1: $2$ coffee. Cup 2: $2$ coffee, $4$ cream ($6$ oz).

check.q: How much liquid is in cup 2 after the first pour?

steps.title: Second pour
steps.explain: Half of cup 2: $1$ coffee $+2$ cream. Cup 1: $3$ coffee, $2$ cream; cream fraction $\tfrac25$.

check.q: What fraction of $3$ coffee $+2$ cream is cream?

solution: After pour 1: cup 2 is $2$ coffee $+4$ cream.
2002A17.shortcut: A small table of amounts avoids all confusion.
2002A17.recognize: Pouring mixtures back and forth: track each ingredient's amount.

2002A18.goal: $27$ dice make a $3\times3\times3$ cube. We want the smallest possible sum of visible faces. Corner dice show $3$ faces, edge dice $2$, face-centre dice $1$; choose the smallest faces each time.

tools.name: Adjacent faces
tools.why: No two of them are opposite (opposites sum to $7$).

2002A18.approach: Corners: $1+2+3=6$ each. Edges: $1+2=3$ each. Face centres: $1$ each. Total $8\cdot6+12\cdot3+6\cdot1$.

steps.title: Per position
steps.explain: $1,2,3$ are mutually adjacent, so corners show $6$; edges show $1+2=3$; centres show $1$.

check.q: Can $1$ and $6$ both be visible on an edge die?

2002A18.bridge: Count positions by visible faces and use the smallest values.
2002A18.shortcut: Check that the smallest numbers can share a vertex: $1,2,3$ can.
2002A18.recognize: Visible faces of a built cube: classify positions as corner/edge/centre.

2002A19.goal: A dog tied with a $2$-yd rope to a vertex of a regular hexagon (side $1$). We want the reachable area outside the hexagon: a big sector plus two small sectors when the rope wraps around the neighbouring corners.

tools.name: Outside angle at a vertex
tools.why: Interior angle of a regular hexagon.

tools.name: Wrapping
tools.why: The exterior angle of a hexagon is $60^\circ$.

2002A19.approach: Big sector: $\tfrac{240}{360}\cdot\pi\cdot4=\tfrac{8\pi}3$. Two small sectors: $2\cdot\tfrac{60}{360}\cdot\pi\cdot1=\tfrac\pi3$. Total $3\pi$.

check.q: What fraction of a circle is $240^\circ$?

2002A19.bridge: Big sector plus two wrap-around sectors.
2002A19.shortcut: Rope length $2$ = two sides, so the wrap stops before reaching the next vertex beyond.
2002A19.recognize: Tethered animals around polygons: sectors that shrink as the rope wraps corners.

2002A20.goal: $A,\ldots,F$ are equally spaced (gap $1$) on a line; $G$ is off it, $H$ on $GD$, $J$ on $GF$, with $HC\parallel JE\parallel AG$. We want $\tfrac{HC}{JE}$. Use similar triangles with $AG$.
2002A20.shortcut: Parallel segments to a common side scale with their distance from the shared vertex.
traps: Measuring from $A$ instead of from $D$ and $F$.
2002A20.recognize: Several parallel segments in a triangle: each is a scaled copy of the base.

2002A21.goal: Eight integers with mean, median, unique mode and range all $8$. We want the largest possible element $M$. Sum is $64$ and the minimum is $M-8$; make the other numbers as small as possible.
2002A21.approach: Try $6,6,6,8,8,8,8,14$: sum $64$, median $8$, mode $8$ (four times beats three), range $8$. For $M=15$, the minimum $7$ forces six middle numbers summing to $42$, i.e. all $7$, which breaks the median.

check.q: Why can the three $6$s coexist with the mode $8$?

steps.title: Rule out $15$
steps.explain: With $M=15$: minimum $7$, the other six sum to $64-15-7=42$, each $\ge7$, so all are $7$. Then the median is $7$, not $8$.

2002A21.bridge: Build a $14$ example; show $15$ is impossible.
solution: $M=15$ forces all middle values to be $7$: contradiction.
2002A21.shortcut: To maximise one element under a fixed sum, push all others to their lower bounds.
traps: Ignoring the range condition on the minimum.
2002A21.recognize: Extremal statistics: fix the sum and push other values to their bounds.

2002A22.goal: Start with $100$ tiles; each step removes the perfect-square-numbered tiles ($\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ of them) and renumbers. We want the number of steps to reach $1$ tile.
2002A22.approach: From $k^2$ it takes exactly $2$ steps to reach $(k-1)^2$. From $10^2$ down to $1^2$: $9$ drops, $18$ steps.

check.q: From $90$ tiles, how many are removed?

2002A22.shortcut: Write out the first few: $100,90,81,72,64$ — the pattern is clear.
2002A22.recognize: Repeated removal by a rule: find what happens between perfect squares.

2002A23.goal: On a line $A,B,C,D$ with $AB=CD=x$, $BC=12$; $E$ above with $BE=CE=10$. Perimeter $AED$ is twice perimeter $BEC$. We want $x$.

check.q: What is the perimeter of $\triangle BEC$?

2002A23.bridge: Write $AE$ with the altitude $8$ and solve.
2002A23.recognize: Symmetric points on a line with an apex: drop the altitude and use Pythagoras.

2002A24.goal: Tina picks $2$ distinct numbers from $1$–$5$; Sergio picks from $1$–$10$. We want $P(\text{Sergio}>\text{Tina's sum})$. Average over Tina's $10$ pairs.
2002A24.bridge: For each pair, count Sergio's winning numbers.
2002A24.shortcut: Average sum is $6$; $P\approx\tfrac{10-6}{10}=\tfrac25$ exactly, since $P$ is linear in $s$.
traps: Allowing Tina to pick the same number twice.
2002A24.recognize: Comparing two random quantities: condition on the one with fewer outcomes.

2002A25.goal: Trapezoid with bases $52$ and $39$, legs $12$ and $5$. We want the area, so we need the height. Slide the legs together to form a triangle.

tools.name: Leg triangle
tools.why: The base difference $52-39=13$ with the two legs.

tools.name: Height
tools.why: Altitude to the hypotenuse of a $5$-$12$-$13$ right triangle.

2002A25.approach: Translate one leg to meet the other: triangle $5,12,13$, right-angled. Its altitude to the side $13$ is the trapezoid's height. Area $=\tfrac{52+39}2\cdot\tfrac{60}{13}$.

check.q: What is the altitude to the hypotenuse of a $5$-$12$-$13$ triangle?

2002A25.bridge: Form the leg triangle to get the height.
solution: Legs with base difference form a $5$-$12$-$13$ triangle.
traps: Using a leg as the height.
2002A25.recognize: Trapezoid with all four sides known: slide legs together to get a triangle.
